front.title: Directwire — An Identity-Centric Transport for Autonomous Agents

abstract.t: This document specifies Directwire, a transport and discovery protocol in which a peer's cryptographic identity is its address. A Directwire node registers a set of candidate network endpoints with a lightweight relay that brokers NAT traversal; once a direct path is established, peers communicate peer-to-peer without any intermediary. Session establishment supports a default ephemeral-DH handshake (X25519 + Ed25519) and an optional hybrid national-crypto / post-quantum channel (SM2 + ML-KEM-768 with an SM4-GCM data plane). Messages carry monotonic sequence numbers with a sliding replay window. Path selection scores candidate paths by RTT and loss with hysteresis.

Directwire is designed for autonomous agents: long-lived, unattended programs that need a stable address that cannot be taken away by a broker or a cloud relay, direct connectivity when NAT permits, and a secure fallback when it does not. This document is an informational draft describing the protocol as implemented by the reference implementation at version 0.2.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: Autonomous agents today are chained to central brokers and cloud relays. Their "address" is a session in someone else's database: revocable, rate-limited, and subject to the availability and policy of the broker. Directwire replaces that dependency with a cryptographic identity that cannot be taken away. Peers are dialed by public key, not by IP.
The protocol has four design goals:

li.t: Identity is the address. A node is dialed by the 32-byte Ed25519 public key that is its Node ID. No DNS, no registry, and no IP is the primary identity.

Encrypted by default, hybrid-hardened. Sessions are encrypted. The optional hybrid channel layers a national-crypto signature scheme (SM2) and a post-quantum key-encapsulation mechanism (ML-KEM-768) so that breaking the session requires breaking both components.
Direct when possible, relayed when not. NAT hole punching establishes a peer-to-peer path; a relay guarantees liveness as a fallback. A late or failed punch never wedges a session.
Adaptive paths. Route selection weighs RTT and loss with hysteresis so that paths do not flap under real-world jitter.

section.t: The Directwire wire format described here is the shared contract across the Directwire protocol family. Companion documents (not yet drafted) describe the message-oriented RPC transport, the low-latency media transport, and the edge data plane.
Directwire's candidate-discovery and relay-brokering design follows the iroh peer-to-peer model . This document was produced using the xml2rfc version 3 vocabulary .

section.name: Key Words
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

li.t: Byte order is big-endian unless otherwise noted.
Domain-separated protocol labels are fixed ASCII byte strings. They are part of the wire contract: changing a label is a breaking change and MUST be accompanied by a version bump.

dl.dd: A Directwire endpoint holding an Ed25519 key pair.
The 32-byte Ed25519 public key of a node. It is the address used for dialing.
A network address (interface address or observed address) at which a node may be reachable.
A server that forwards encrypted traffic between peers that cannot establish a direct path and brokers candidate exchange.
A peer-to-peer path established after successful NAT traversal.
A negotiated, encrypted channel between two nodes, keyed by a session ID derived from the handshake transcript.

li.t: Each node has an Ed25519 key pair ; the Node ID is the 32-byte Ed25519 public key and is the address used for dialing.

A node MAY additionally hold an SM2 static key bound to the Ed25519 Node ID via a BIND signature (Section ). The binding prevents an active man-in-the-middle from splicing a different SM2 key into the same identity.

Identity is public-key-first: no DNS, no registry, no revocation list in the base protocol. Trust is established by key pinning or out-of-band fingerprint verification. The reference implementation uses trust-on-first-use (TOFU); production deployments SHOULD pre-pin peer public keys.

section.name: Transport Overview
section.t: The default transport is UDP. A node binds zero or more candidate endpoints (local interface addresses and observed addresses). A relay provides liveness: it forwards encrypted traffic between peers that cannot establish a direct path, and it brokers candidate exchange.

section.name: Relay Control Frames
section.t: The relay connection is a TCP stream. Frames are length-prefixed: a 32-bit big-endian length followed by the payload. The following control frames are defined:

tr.td: STUN-like echo of the peer's TCP source address
ask the relay to broker both sides' candidates
relay cross-sends the peer's candidate set
forwarded ciphertext; from is overwritten from the connection identity (anti-spoofing)
e.g. "first frame must be Hello", "target is not online", "recipient is not online"

section.t: Candidate addresses carry a type tag: CAND_PUNCH (hole-punch UDP) and CAND_QUIC (direct QUIC). The relay MUST overwrite the from field of RelayData from the authenticated connection identity, so that a sender cannot spoof another node's identity.

li.t: Peers exchange candidate endpoints via the relay (Exchange); the STUN-like observed address (Section ) is included.

Each side sends PUNCH UDP packets to the peer's candidate set. A PUNCH packet is a 4-byte magic PMP1 followed by a 32-byte Node ID; the receiver dispatches it to the matching state machine by sender Node ID.
On receiving a PUNCH from a candidate address, a peer establishes the direct path and replies.
Failure or late arrival of a PUNCH MUST NOT wedge the session: the state machine falls back to the relay path.
After completion, a small reply budget (default 5 per peer) answers late PUNCH packets so that an asymmetric peer can finish.

section.name: Default (Relay Path) Handshake — X25519 + Ed25519
section.t: A two-message handshake over the relay channel, Noise-IK-style ephemeral DH with identity signatures ; the ephemeral key exchange uses X25519 and the identity signatures use Ed25519 :

tr.td: HS_TAG (0x48), HS_KIND_INIT (0x01), ephemeral X25519 pk (32B), NodeId (32B), Ed25519 signature
HS_TAG (0x48), HS_KIND_RESP (0x02), ephemeral X25519 pk (32B), NodeId (32B), Ed25519 signature, AEAD envelope

section.t: On success, transport keys are split from the DH shared secret and the identities; the transcript hash becomes the session ID. A ciphertext arriving before the handshake completes is dropped.

section.name: Optional GM-PQ Channel
section.t: When enabled on both sides, the relay path uses a hybrid handshake: SM2 + ML-KEM-768 hybrid KEM , an SM3 transcript , and an SM4-GCM data plane . Channel frames are relay payloads tagged with a leading GM_TAG (0x47):

tr.td: wake the peer and signal GM-PQ intent
client echoes the cookie and retries MSG1
client final (hybrid ciphertext + AEAD identity + SM2 signature)

section.t: Role rule. The smaller Node ID is the client (initiator), and the larger is the server (responder); simultaneous initiation is naturally deduplicated.

Identity binding. After the handshake both sides send BIND as the first ciphertext: BND1 + Ed25519 Node ID + a signature over b"p2p-mesh/gmpq-bind" || SM3(gm_pk) || node_id || session_id. The handshake layer is TOFU (SM2 keys are not pre-authenticated), but BIND strongly binds the session to the authenticated Ed25519 identity: a man-in-the-middle splicing two half-handshakes would obtain different session IDs, so a forwarded BIND is rejected. Production SHOULD replace TOFU with a pinned SM2 anchor.

Fallback. If the peer has GM-PQ off, channel frames are silently ignored; after a 3-second timeout the implementation falls back to the Section X25519 handshake. A generation-tagged timer prevents stale-fire.
Forward secrecy. Breaking the hybrid session requires breaking both the classical (SM2) and the post-quantum (ML-KEM-768) components (X-Wing/GHP18 combiner, SM3 as random oracle).

section.name: Direct Path — QUIC/TLS 1.3
section.t: The QUIC endpoint, secured with TLS 1.3 , self-signs a certificate whose public key equals the Node ID. The connecting side pins the certificate to the expected Node ID (dial-by-public-key); the server side validates structural validity only. ALPN = b"p2p-mesh/0", SAN node.p2p-mesh.local. Hole punching and QUIC run on the same UDP socket, so the opened NAT mapping serves both. Simultaneous open: both sides connect and accept; the smaller Node ID's outbound connection is canonical, and duplicates are closed with b"duplicate" or b"superseded".

section.name: Message Framing
section.t: The message-oriented data plane follows Homa's receiver-driven design , with message-level (not byte-stream) semantics. The framing rules are:

li.t: Messages carry a monotonically increasing 64-bit sequence number used as AEAD nonce entropy.
The receiver maintains a 64-slot sliding replay window: duplicate or too-old sequence numbers are rejected; reordering of up to 64 messages is allowed (suitable for UDP and multi-path).
Relay inner plaintexts are tagged: INNER_DATA (0x01) application message, INNER_PING (0x02) and INNER_PONG (0x03) keepalive probes.
Paths are scored by RTT and loss. Effective score = RTT * (1 + 10 * loss), with hysteresis and a minimum dwell time to prevent flapping.
Path states are relay (initial) and direct (after punch), with fallback to relay if the direct path degrades or drops. Switching is seamless: queued messages are flushed over the new path.
0-RTT early data has no full forward secrecy and MAY be replayed within the crash window; applications MUST treat early data as idempotent.
The relay sees only ciphertext. The relay cannot decrypt, authenticate, or inspect agent traffic; it only forwards and meters.
Post-quantum readiness. Breaking the hybrid session requires breaking both the classical (SM2/ECDH) and the post-quantum (ML-KEM-768) components.

Reference implementation scope. The cryptographic modules are an architecture-validation skeleton and are NOT formally certified. Deployments subject to commercial-crypto regulation MUST perform their own certification and evaluation before use.
The relay control-plane protocol described in Section predates authentication of the relay stream in the base protocol; operators SHOULD deploy the relay behind transport security (e.g. TLS).

section.name: IANA Considerations
section.t: This document has no IANA actions. If the protocol matures to the Standards Track, the protocol labels, candidate tags, and inner plaintext tags defined here should be registered.

section.name: v0.3 Candidate — Explicit DONE Message Replacing Implicit ACK
section.t: Status: design note / candidate. Not part of the current wire format (v0.2).

section.name: Background: The Short-Message Loss Dead-Zone (v0.2 Problem)
section.t: For messages entirely within the unscheduled window (under 10 KB), the receiver issues no GRANT and reassembles the message from the first packet(s) alone. If such a message's first packet is lost, the receiver has never seen the message and therefore cannot send RESEND; the sender cannot know the message is lost without some acknowledgment.

v0.2 closes this with an implicit ACK: the RPC response doubles as the request's acknowledgment. The transport keeps the finished request in a retransmit window (retransmit_timeout, conservative RTT estimate, default 500 ms) and re-sends chunk 0 if no confirm() arrived; the receiver uses the re-sent chunk 0 to (re)establish reassembly and drive the rest via GRANT/RESEND. This is entirely sender-side (no wire change) and provably adds zero extra traffic when there is no loss.

section.name: Why a Candidate at All
section.t: The implicit-ACK design has three structural costs:

li.t: Response loss is handled at the RPC layer, not the transport. If the response is lost, the request's transport message is confirmed anyway, and recovery falls to the client's at-least-once retry (attempt_timeout) plus server idempotent replay. The RPC layer must keep attempt_timeout > retransmit_timeout + RTT to avoid racing the sender's own poke — a coupling the transport should not need.
Only RPC requests get the window. Responses do not retransmit; a response whose first packet is lost must wait for the client to re-request. The transport is not self-contained.
confirm() is an RPC-layer concept. The transport cannot tell "delivered" from "still in flight" without being told by an upper layer.
Add a DONE control message sent by the receiver once it has reassembled a complete message: msg_id plus an optional cumulative fingerprint/checksum.

The sender treats DONE as the release condition: the message is removed from its state immediately (no linger, no retransmit window) — the wire now carries explicit delivery confirmation instead of inferring it from an application response.

This makes request and response loss symmetric: both are transport-confirmed, and the RPC layer's attempt_timeout becomes a pure backstop for a lost DONE (recoverable by the existing at-least-once retry) rather than the primary recovery path.
Wire change: new packet type, version/label bump (Section ). v0.2 deliberately kept the wire format untouched (sender-only fix).
More receiver state: must track delivered message IDs to emit DONE and avoid DONE-storms on reordered delivery.
DONE loss handling: a lost DONE reintroduces the window it was meant to remove — it needs its own re-request or timeout, trading one acknowledgment mechanism for another.

Idempotent-replay value proposition unchanged: at-least-once semantics already make application-level dedup mandatory; DONE removes transport reliance on it but does not remove the application requirement.
